head.title: AI for XSLT and XPath: Copilot and Claude Code in VS Code

div.p: AI coding assistants in Visual Studio Code - such as GitHub Copilot or Claude Code - can make good use of the XSLT/XPath extension. Most of what they use needs nothing special from it: the extension's problems, documentation notes and debugging output are all in forms that assistants read and write well. For more, the extension has an MCP server, so an assistant can ask it directly - for example, for the problems of a stylesheet that isn't open, where a function is declared, or what an XPath expression finds in your XML - and a skill that tells the assistant how to use those tools well.

The problems reported by the extension's linter are standard Visual Studio Code diagnostics, shown in the Problems view. They identify the exact symbol at issue - an unresolved variable, a function called with the wrong number of arguments, a record field that doesn't exist - so an assistant that reads the diagnostics can explain and fix them precisely, and check its own changes the same way. For example, GitHub Copilot can include the problems with #problems in a chat prompt, or fix a problem from its Quick Fix menu, and Claude Code reads them through its Visual Studio Code integration.

The problems are kept up to date for every stylesheet open in an editor - not only the active one. An assistant usually changes files while your cursor is in another, so a stylesheet it changes is checked again, whether it's shown beside the active editor or in a tab that isn't shown, and the assistant sees the problems its change caused. When it changes several stylesheets at once, each is checked with its own declarations, XSLT version and imports, so no problems are reported that aren't there.

The extension can run a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, with tools an assistant can call to ask the extension about your stylesheets. The tools use the same code as the editor - the linter, Go to Definition, Find All References and the XSLT Imports view - so their answers match what you see, and they work for files that aren't open. The server is off by default: to turn it on, set XSLT.mcp.enabled to true - see Settings. With it on, the server starts with the window for a workspace that contains XSLT, XSpec or Schematron files, without one being opened first - and for any other workspace, when an XML or XSLT file is opened.

tr.td: The problems in an XSLT module or XSpec file - as the Problems view shows them, checked with its imports, includes and packages - whether or not it's open. Optionally, only those of a severity or worse. A module that another stylesheet imports or includes is checked with that top-level stylesheet's declarations too, as in the editor: the one found for it in the workspace, or one the assistant gives - for example, a stylesheet outside the workspace.

The problems in each XSLT and XSpec file in a folder: a summary, then only the files with problems. By default, warnings and errors - not hints, such as unused variables. Files in hidden folders, such as .git, and those the files.exclude setting hides aren't checked.
The tree of imports, includes and packages from a module's top-level stylesheet down, with the module marked - as in the XSLT Imports view.

Every function, named template, global variable and parameter, mode, key, attribute set, accumulator, item type and character map a module can use: its own, then those of the modules and packages it imports, includes or uses - each with its parameters and types, its location, and the first line of its documentation, and one overridden by a higher import precedence marked. An assistant calls it before writing or changing a stylesheet, to reuse what exists. Optionally, only one kind; as for lint_file, the top-level stylesheet can be given.

Evaluates an XPath expression on an XML file with your Saxon jar - the program behind Find Nodes with XPath, in a process of its own - and gives the number of items and the first 100 as the debugger shows values: a node as its path, a map or array in full. An assistant uses it on a stylesheet's source XML to check its structure, a match pattern or a select expression, before writing templates. XPath 4.0 by default, or 3.1 - with Saxon-HE, which can't evaluate 4.0, 3.1 is used. It's evaluated as in a stylesheet, so a result isn't better than the stylesheet's: unprefixed element names are in no namespace, whatever the document's default namespace - unless the assistant gives the stylesheet's xpath-default-namespace, and an empty result says when that may be why. The prefixes the document declares are bound. To use another prefix, the assistant puts a declare namespace line for it at the very start, each ending in a semicolon: declare namespace o = 'urn:orders'; declare namespace x = 'urn:x'; //o:order/x:ref. Those lines are the only thing allowed before the XPath - it is XPath, not XQuery, so there is no declare variable, declare function or default element namespace (the xpathDefaultNamespace argument gives that). xs, fn, map, array, math and err are predeclared (a stylesheet has to declare map, array and math). Errors are given with Saxon's code and position. Each node found is listed with the line and column where it starts in the XML file - from the extension's own outline of it, as Find Nodes goes there, not Saxon's saxon:line-number(), which is where the start tag ends. The saxon: extension functions need Saxon-PE or Saxon-EE, not Saxon-HE. Needs the XSLT.tasks.saxonJar setting. Requests run one at a time, so an assistant that sends several at once gets each answered, and an expression that takes more than 30 seconds is stopped and reported as such.
What it can't do: for safety - an expression can otherwise run programs - it has no extension functions (calls to Java, or EXPath modules such as file:), no collection() or uri-collection(), no http: addresses, and doc() and unparsed-text() read only files in the workspace folders and beside the XML file - not through a symbolic link out of them. The XML file's external entities aren't read.

Where a function, named template, global variable or parameter, mode, key, attribute set, accumulator, item type or character map is declared, as seen from a module - with its parameters and types, and its documentation: its documentation note, or a comment just before it. When more than one module declares it, the one used, with the highest import precedence, is first. As for lint_file, the assistant can give the top-level stylesheet the module is seen from.

The references to one of these, as Find All References finds them - in the modules that use it and the XSpec files that test it - with each reference's line. The XSpec uses are listed last, as the tests, each with the scenario it's in.
An XSLT 4.0 named item type: a record type's fields, with their types and @field documentation, or an enumeration type's values - with a top-level stylesheet given, as for find_declaration.
The signature and description of a built-in XPath or XSLT function, for XPath 3.1 or 4.0 - for a function declared in a stylesheet, the assistant uses find_declaration.

How you run stylesheets: the Saxon jar, with its edition, version and licence, the XML catalog, the XSpec installation and the XSLT packages - and for a stylesheet, its Quick Run: the XML context file, the parameters, and the exact java command line, with the options the extension adds, such as -catalog and -lib. An assistant that runs Saxon itself then gets the same result as you.

div.p: The tools only read files: they don't change them, or run stylesheets or tests - an assistant runs run_configuration's command itself, if you allow it. evaluate_xpath only evaluates an expression on an XML file.

With the server on, Copilot finds it by itself: its tools are listed with the other MCP tools in Copilot Chat's agent mode. There's no need to add it to an mcp.json file - it would then be listed twice, and with a token that XSLT: Reset MCP Server Token would make out of date.

Visual Studio Code's MCP: List Servers command lists the server as XSLT/XPath: choose it to start, stop or restart it, to see its tools, or to show its output. The first time it starts, Visual Studio Code may ask you to trust it. When a new release of the extension adds tools, Visual Studio Code finds them the next time the server starts. The server also gives Copilot the xslt-xpath skill.

Run XSLT: Set Up MCP Server for Claude Code from the Command Palette - it offers to turn the server on, if it isn't, and asks whether to set it up for this project - recommended, with a window for each project - or for all your projects, which then use this window's server. Run it in each project's window. It runs Claude Code's claude mcp add command for you. A Claude Code session started after that can use the tools, whether it runs in Visual Studio Code or in a terminal of its own. A session already running keeps the settings it started with, so /mcp doesn't connect it: start a new one - in Visual Studio Code, a new conversation in the Claude panel.

If the claude command isn't found - for example, it isn't on the path Visual Studio Code uses - the claude mcp add command is copied instead: run it in a terminal - for one project, in that project's folder.

In a workspace with several folders, choose the folder that Claude Code is started in. The server can see all the folders, and the tools' relative paths - and the paths they show - are from that folder, not the workspace's first. The set-up is for one folder: to use Claude Code in another folder of the workspace, run the command again and choose it. A folder added to the workspace later needs the same - the server itself doesn't change. The assistant is told the paths of the workspace's folders when it connects - and run_configuration lists them - so it can check a file in any of them.
div.aside: These choices are about which Claude Code sessions use the server, and where its relative paths start - not what it can reach. The window's server serves all of its workspace folders however it's set up, and a tool given an absolute path can check any file. What protects your files is the token and the local-only connection, described below.
div.p: The extension has a skill, xslt-xpath: a set of instructions an assistant loads when a task needs it, here any work on XSLT, XSpec or XPath. It tells the assistant how to use the tools above together:

ul.li: find the XSLT version and never raise it, and look up what a module already declares before writing a second copy of a function (list_declarations);
check each change with lint_file, read warnings that come from imports it can't resolve, and not make a package component public just to silence an error;
run the stylesheet and its XSpec tests with the command from run_configuration, rather than a Saxon command of its own;

the habits that avoid common errors - such as writing < for < in XPath in an attribute, and a global variable that uses the context item, which the linter can't report - and to say afterwards what it linted, ran and tested.

div.p: How the assistant gets it depends on the assistant:

ul.li: GitHub Copilot, in Visual Studio Code 1.147 or later - the server serves the skill itself, as skills over MCP (a Beta extension of the protocol), so there is nothing to install and it is always the version that goes with the server's tools. Visual Studio Code may ask you to allow the skill into the model's context the first time it connects to the server. It is listed under the server on the Skills tab of the Agent Customizations editor. To turn off skills from all MCP servers, use Visual Studio Code's chat.agentHost.mcpSkills.enabled setting. In an earlier version of Visual Studio Code, Copilot still has all the server's tools, but not the skill.

Claude Code - XSLT: Set Up MCP Server for Claude Code also installs the skill in ~/.claude/skills (or in the folder CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR names) - for all your projects, as it only applies where the server is connected. It is kept up to date with the extension: each time the server starts, a copy the extension installed is replaced by the new version. A copy you have edited, or a skill of that name that came from elsewhere, is left as it is - to keep your changes, edit a copy under another name.
Other assistants - those that support skills over MCP get it from the server in the same way; the others get the tools without the skill.

div.p: The server only accepts connections from your own computer (127.0.0.1), and each request needs a token that the extension makes once and keeps in Visual Studio Code's secret storage - it doesn't expire. Claude Code keeps the token in its own settings; a copied claude mcp add command includes it, so keep the command private. To make a new token - for example, if the old one has been shared - run XSLT: Reset MCP Server Token. Copilot uses the new token straight away, and Claude Code is set up again with it - for all projects, or for a project in the workspace - where it was set up with the old one. A Claude Code session already running keeps the old token: start a new one.

Each Visual Studio Code window has a server of its own, for its workspace, so with a window for each project, an assistant started in a project's folder uses that project's window. Its tools work best for the files of that workspace: a relative path is taken from its first folder, and a module's top-level stylesheet is found from the workspace's modules. A window's port is the same each time its workspace is opened - one of the 999 after XSLT.mcp.port (6745 by default), chosen for the workspace, or the next free one if another program has it; if it ever changes, Claude Code set up for the project is set up again with it. A window with no folder open uses XSLT.mcp.port itself. The XSLT MCP Server output channel shows each window's address, or why its server didn't start.

XSLT 4.0 documentation notes - xsl:note format="xdoc-md" - use Markdown with @param and @return tags, in the style of Javadoc: a format that assistants already know. An assistant can read a function's note to understand it, and can write notes too - for example, when asked to document the functions in a stylesheet. As the extension checks the @param tags against the parameters, a missing or misnamed parameter in a note is reported straight away.

The output of xdm:debug() in xsl:message is plain, labelled text: each variable's value in XPath syntax, with its type where it isn't obvious, and each node with its path. Copied from the terminal into a chat, it gives an assistant the actual values to reason about, rather than a description of the problem.

Quick Run creates ordinary tasks in the workspace's tasks.json file, and each task shows the Saxon command line it runs in the terminal. An assistant that can run commands can run a transform in the same way.

Visual Studio Code's Agents window, for running agent sessions and reviewing their changes, only runs the extensions on a list chosen by Microsoft, and the XSLT/XPath extension isn't on it yet. Without the extension, XSLT files in the Agents window have plain XML highlighting, with none of the extension's features - and if Red Hat's XML extension is installed, it may report errors against its XSLT 3.0 schema. To run the extension in the Agents window, add this to your user settings - see Settings:

The MCP server's tools only read files: an assistant can't yet ask the extension to run a stylesheet or an XSpec test, though it can run the Saxon command that run_configuration gives, or a Quick Run task's, itself - and the skill tells it to. An XPath expression it can evaluate with evaluate_xpath, within the limits described there. Tools for running stylesheets and tests may be added in a future release.

In the Problems view, problems are only shown for files open in an editor, as by most language extensions: a stylesheet an assistant changes that isn't open has none there until it's opened. With the MCP server on, an assistant can check such a file with lint_file.
